investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design
investigations.hardware: ACME burner flames in the CIR
investigations.objective: The primary objectives of this flight experiment are: A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames. B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames. C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.

needs.basis: Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. [...] Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames.

investigations.how_tests_differ: Flames burned on a 6.35 mm porous spherical burner. Round 1 (2019) gave normal flames: ethylene, pure or nitrogen-diluted, flowing into oxygen-nitrogen ambients of 21 to 40% oxygen. Round 2 (2021-22) began with one normal propane day, then inverse flames: oxygen-nitrogen flowing into an ethylene ambient. Tests varied flow rate (some ramped), where the nitrogen was placed and so the stoichiometric mixture fraction, and pressure (logs mention 0.5 to 1.3 atm). CO2 diluent and methane were not used. Precursor tests used 2.2 and 5.2 s drop towers.
investigations.relevance: NASA states ACME's gas-flame experiments target energy and environmental goals, not spacecraft fire safety. Indirectly, the results show that weak spherical microgravity flames can burn steadily for minutes and extinguish only near 1130 K, and that sooting appeared mainly at 40% oxygen, which bears on flammability limits and smoke signatures in oxygen-enriched atmospheres.

findings.statement: Across normal and inverse flames, radiative extinction occurred at a common critical peak flame temperature near 1130 K and a fixed reactant mass flux, matching the investigation's second hypothesis.
The ISS tests showed that burner-stabilized spherical diffusion flames can reach a steady state, with a characteristic time to steady state of about 100,000 s.
Long-duration flames grow, heat the burner, and can show oscillatory partial extinction.
Sooting depended strongly on oxygen: constantly sooting flames appeared only at 40% oxygen with high fuel concentration, while small and large flames in 21% oxygen did not soot.

Drop-tower work behind the flight design found that flame structure, set by moving inert between oxidizer and fuel (stoichiometric mixture fraction), dominates soot behaviour over the direction of convection.
Because weak microgravity flames go out only near 1100-1130 K, below normal-gravity extinction temperatures, a weak flame in orbit may keep burning where 1-g experience would predict extinction.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator
investigations.hardware: ACME burner flames in the CIR
investigations.objective: The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties. The specific flight objectives are as follows. 1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels. 2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired). 3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

needs.basis: While it burned gaseous fuels, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project was a study of materials flammability in still atmospheres as a function of material properties.

investigations.how_tests_differ: Every test burned gaseous fuel on a flat porous burner in a quiescent chamber, with no imposed flow. Tests varied burner diameter (25 mm in round 1; 25 and 50 mm in round 2), fuel (ethylene, pure or 50% in nitrogen, and methane on the 25 mm burner), fuel mass flux (about 1 to 12 g/m2s), oxygen in nitrogen (0.21 to 0.40) and pressure (about 0.565 to 1 bar). Planned O2/CO2 ambients were not run. Normal-gravity and 5 s drop tests served as comparisons.
investigations.relevance: Stopping ventilation, an established step in putting out spacecraft fires, may not extinguish a fire in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, where emulated PMMA and Nylon flames kept burning. NASA suggests wider use of flammability Test 2 (cone calorimeter), which measures the material properties that correspond to these microgravity flames.

findings.statement: Quasi-steady burning of a flat surface in a quiescent microgravity atmosphere was achieved at oxygen mole fractions of 0.265 and above, and pressure had only a weak effect.

Flames emulating condensed materials such as PMMA and Nylon kept burning without any air flow, notably in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, while in 21% oxygen they self-extinguished in a short time.

Extinction is tied to a critical flame temperature of about 1100 to 1200 K, which bounds the microgravity flammability maps with two limits: radiative extinction of large flames and heat-loss extinction of small flames.

The flames were blue and soot-free, so their radiation came from gaseous products; steady flames radiated no more than about 60% of their energy, and the radiant fraction correlated with flame height.

The flammability map indicates that 25 mm surfaces with heat of combustion 23.6 to 47.2 kJ/g and heat of gasification 1 to 10 kJ/g can burn steadily; lower fuel fraction and higher oxygen favour longer burns.
Interpreted for real materials, plastics burn more easily but more slowly in microgravity: PE and PP near 3 g/m2s, nylon and PMMA near 2.5 g/m2s, far below their normal-gravity burning fluxes.

investigations.hardware: ACME burner flames in the CIR
investigations.objective: In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives: A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits. B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions.

investigations.how_tests_differ: Over 32 test days (day codes 17319 to 21062), CLD Flame burned coflow diffusion flames of methane and of ethylene, plus a set of improved coflow tests. investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.hardware: ACME burner flames in the CIR
investigations.objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current, analyze the dynamic response of flames to electric field changes, evaluate soot formation, and characterize stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
investigations.how_tests_differ: Two 2018 ISS rounds used different burners: a coflow burner (round 1) and a 2.1 mm gas-jet burner (round 2). Across tests NASA varied the fuel (methane or ethylene, pure or nitrogen-diluted from 30 to 100%), fuel velocity, whether a 21% oxygen coflow was supplied, mesh electrode polarity, and the applied voltage, swept in steps up to 10 kV. First-phase tests ran at 100 kPa. Precursor 1-g and 2.2 s drop-tower tests compared gravity levels.
investigations.relevance: NASA states E-FIELD Flames is not conducted for space applications, and ACME's gas-flame experiments other than BRE target energy and emissions rather than spacecraft fire safety. Any fire-safety value is indirect: microgravity data on how electric fields change near-limit flame stability, soot and extinction, and on ion current as a flame-state signal.

findings.statement: The experiment rests on chemi-ions made in hydrocarbon flames: an applied field drives them, producing an ion-driven wind that acts as a body force on the gas and can be used to measure and reshape a flame without buoyancy.

Long-duration microgravity was needed to separate the ion wind from buoyancy: the 2.2 s drop tower is too short for flames to reach steady state, and a quasi-steady voltage-current sweep takes over 100 s.
In microgravity the flame's ion current rises to a distinct peak as the applied voltage increases and then drops sharply, instead of the saturation plateau seen in 1-g.
The applied field stabilized very dilute, near-limit flames, especially when no air coflow was supplied.
Field polarity sets the response: a positive field compresses the flame and its soot and led to an unpredicted oscillation before extinction, while a negative field keeps the flame near spherical.
Burner geometry changes the electrical response: the gas-jet burner gave a clear parabolic rise of ion current with oscillations that the coflow burner did not show.

investigations.how_tests_differ: s-Flame issued gaseous fuel through a 6.35 mm porous spherical burner into a quiescent oxidizer in ISS microgravity. Fuels were hydrogen, methane, hydrogen/methane blends and ethylene, diluted with nitrogen in round 1 (Sept 2019-Jan 2020) and with helium in round 2 (May-July 2020); ambients were about 21% or 30% oxygen. Fuel flow (planned 1 to 15 cc/s) was held, stepped or ramped up and down to reach radiative and kinetic extinction. CO2 dilution was left for a possible third round.
investigations.relevance: NASA's ACME documents give energy and emissions as the main aim and say it is not aimed at spacecraft fire safety, though one overview slide cites fire safety and the s-Flame final report lists extinction understanding with fire-safety implications. Its value here is foundational: kinetic and radiative extinction limits of gas flames in still microgravity, and how diluents shift them.

findings.statement: Both kinetic extinction (low Damkohler number) and radiative extinction (high Damkohler number) were observed in nitrogen-diluted methane and ethylene spherical flames, the dual extinction limits the experiment was built to map.
The investigators' framework treats diffusion-flame extinction as reactant leakage through the flame; other losses such as radiation act by lowering the flame temperature and so raising leakage.
Nitrogen-diluted hydrogen flames showed kinetic extinction when the fuel flow was ramped down but no radiative extinction.
Switching the diluent from nitrogen to helium shifted the extinction limits and made the spherical flames harder to ignite.

Of the planned regimes, transient spherical flames were obtained but no characteristically sooty ones, and the unstable behaviour seen was near the burner tube rather than the predicted pulsating instability.
Hardware limited the data: at high flow the porous-sphere flames became non-spherical and offset, and a leak of the first fuel bottle meant a planned H2/CH4/N2 blend was not tested.

investigations.how_tests_differ: Glovebox flow-duct tests varied the solid fuel and geometry (thin PMMA films 0.1 to 0.4 mm, PMMA slabs 1 to 5 mm burning on one or two sides, clear and black PMMA rods of three diameters, a PMMA sphere section, Nomex, a wax candle, cotton-fiberglass fabric), sample width, flow direction (opposed, concurrent, stagnation), flow speed (about 1 to 55 cm/s) and oxygen, lowered from about 22% to 13.6% by diluting the glovebox with nitrogen at cabin pressure. Ground tunnels and 5.18 s drop tests gave normal-gravity comparisons.
investigations.relevance: NASA says BASS-II helps engineers select the safest materials and improve firefighting methods, and that its results feed the models used to design fire detection and suppression systems. The tests map where solids stop burning as flow speed and oxygen fall, and show microgravity ignition delays up to ten times the NASA-STD-6001 igniter time.

findings.statement: Over thin PMMA in opposed flow, flames underwent radiative extinction when the flow was reduced below a critical velocity of a few cm/s; this velocity does not depend on fuel thickness but rises at lower oxygen.
For PMMA rods, ignition limits lay above the flammability limits, and ignition delays reached up to ten times the igniter time of NASA-STD-6001.

Along the PMMA rod flammability boundary, analysed with a critical Damkohler number formulation, heat losses were negligible on the high-flow blowoff branch but dominated by radiation on the low-flow quenching branch.

Comparing ISS opposed-flow spread with normal-gravity downward spread over PMMA extended the thermal-regime limit to downward spread in air, giving an effective buoyant velocity of about 1.9 cm/s and a thin-to-thick transition thickness of about 5.2 mm.

Opposed-flow tests on PMMA slabs gave the first thick-fuel microgravity spread data: sample width affected spread over the thinner fuels, two-sided burning spread faster, and the FDS model overpredicted spread rates.

Combustion-product sensing showed CO/CO2 ratios well above those of efficient combustion and heat release rates mostly under 100 W; CO diluted into the US Lab would stay below the spacecraft maximum allowable concentration.

findings.statement: In opposed flow the fabric flame quickly reached a steady spread rate at each flow speed, and spread was fastest at an intermediate flow speed rather than at the highest or lowest.
In concurrent flow a limiting flame length and steady spread rate were reached only at low flow speeds, where spread rate rose linearly with flow.
Reducing concurrent flow to around 1 cm/s produced quenching extinction, verifying the low-speed quenching branch of the U-shaped flammability boundary for this fabric.
The fabric showed enhanced flammability in microgravity: with a forced flow it kept spreading against the flow, whereas in normal-gravity air a flame spreading downward (opposed) self-extinguishes.
Ultem and Nomex HT90-40 did not burn in the ISS atmosphere (21 to 22% oxygen, flow around 15 cm/s), as in normal gravity, though the ISS samples were narrower; Nomex-III did burn.

The long-duration flights gave the first detailed transient flame-growth data in purely forced microgravity flow; they validate several theoretical predictions and feed a transient flame growth model.

investigations.title: Cool Flames Investigation
investigations.objective: The objectives of this investigation are to: 1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm. 2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior. 3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics. 4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion.

needs.basis: Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction

investigations.how_tests_differ: Single n-dodecane, n-dodecane/iso-dodecane or farnesane droplets, free-floating or tethered on a fiber, burned in the CIR chamber after a settling period, with no imposed flow. Across tests NASA varied fuel, pressure (0.25 to 5 atm in the final report; 0.5 to 5 atm in the data summary), oxygen mole fraction, the nitrogen diluent with helium partly replacing it, initial droplet size and support, and igniter power and duration.
investigations.relevance: NASA states that cool flames matter for spacecraft fire safety because a cool flame can persist after the hot flame goes out, generate combustible vapour and reignite, much like smouldering. So apparent extinction of a liquid-fuel fire in microgravity may not mean it is out.

findings.statement: Cool flames burn quasi-steadily at about 700 to 900 K in the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) chemistry region, far cooler than hot flames above 1200 K.

FLEX results cited for CFI show that replacing nitrogen with helium raises droplet burning rates and shortens both hot and cool burning, and that fuel matters: n-alkanes show cool flames, methanol does not.

Applied to FLEX droplets, partial-burning theory predicts cool-flame burning rate and flame standoff ratio, and cool-flame extinction diameter correlates with oxygen concentration to the -3/2 power, but the approach fails at higher pressures.

investigations.title: Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2
investigations.objective: The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak, to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process. DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity. Summarized objectives include: 1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity 2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control 3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity 4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments

investigations.relevance: NASA states that longer missions need more reliable and sensitive fire detection; DAFT supported this by qualifying the particle counter SAME used to size smoke for detector design, and by measuring the low particulate background of ISS cabin air.

findings.statement: The commercial P-Trak relies on gravity to return condensed alcohol; using capillary forces in the condenser and removing the mercury orientation switch adapted it for microgravity.

Undisturbed ISS cabin air carries very little particulate, which the team attributes to HEPA filtration.
On orbit the particle count-to-mass ratio fell below the ground relation, which the team reads as larger particles staying airborne in microgravity.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2
investigations.objective: The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models. Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as: 1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets. 2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion. 3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries. 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics. 5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays. 6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments.

investigations.how_tests_differ: FLEX-2 varied six parameters independently: fuel type (pure fuels such as ethanol, decane, heptane, n-octane and iso-octane, plus bi-component and surrogate mixtures), ambient gas (oxygen in nitrogen or helium), pressure (0.5 to 3.0 atm), initial droplet diameter (planned 1.5 to 5 mm), droplet translation velocity for slow convection (planned 0.1 to 5 cm/s), and spacing and size in binary droplet arrays. NASA's approach gives oxygen 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction; the experimental table lists 0.17 to 0.3.
investigations.relevance: NASA frames FLEX-2 as fundamental liquid-fuel combustion for cleaner, more efficient engines and surrogate fuels, returning from FLEX's fire-safety focus. Its fire-safety value is indirect: radiative and diffusive extinction boundaries for new fuels, flammability maps for interacting droplets, and soot data the SRD links to microgravity smoke detection.

findings.statement: The SRD explains two extinction modes: radiative extinction of large flames by radiant loss and diffusive extinction of small flames by conductive loss; the boundary between them was known for heptane but not for ethanol or decane, which FLEX-2 set out to determine.

investigations.title: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.objective: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions.

needs.basis: Suppression was studied in the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) through dilution of the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium, both of which suppress fire.

needs.tier: stated in NASA's objective for the investigation
needs.basis: The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments

investigations.how_tests_differ: FLEX burned single n-heptane or methanol droplets, planned at about 3 and 5 mm initial diameter. Between tests NASA varied ambient pressure (planned 0.5 to 1.5 atm, plus a 2 to 3 atm radiative-environment set), lowered the oxygen mole fraction step by step toward the limiting oxygen index, and added CO2 or helium as suppressant; SF6 was planned, but the flight table lists only CO2 and helium. Droplets were free or fiber-supported, quiescent or slowly translated (planned 1.5 cm/s).
investigations.relevance: NASA states FLEX maps the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity and measures the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants (CO2, He, SF6) to improve fire-safety protocols for space missions; its requirements document links this to the ISS suppressant trade studies that chose CO2 extinguishers and to a flooding goal of bringing oxygen below the limiting oxygen index.

findings.statement: In ISS tests, n-heptane droplets burned with a hot flame, lost the visible flame by radiative extinction, then kept reacting in a cool-flame stage without visible flame that ended in diffusive extinction; a detailed-kinetics model reproduces this.
Simulations in the same study indicate that heat loss initiates the transition to cool-flame burning, and that adding CO2 or helium to the ambient triggers it through enhanced heat loss.

For n-octane and n-decane droplets in air (ISS and drop tower), burning rate and flame standoff ratio fall and soot standoff ratio rises with initial diameter; radiative loss explains the large-droplet trend, and the support fiber raises burning rate for 1-2 mm droplets.

In methanol droplet flames, combustion water condenses into the droplet and later evaporates; the theory presented links this water to a falling flame temperature until the reaction can no longer be sustained.

The requirements document argues that radiative and conductive losses near extinction give a minimum limiting oxygen index at a critical droplet diameter, and that this droplet LOI is a conservative fire-safety limit.

Spacecraft practice stops ventilation on a fire alarm, but the requirements document notes that crew movement and extinguisher discharge induce flows of several to tens of cm/s, leaving open how such flow changes the extinguishing concentration.

investigations.title: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight
investigations.objective: Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments.

needs.basis: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R).

investigations.how_tests_differ: Smoke came from sub-ignition heating of five spacecraft materials: Kapton, Teflon, silicone rubber, lamp wick and Pyrell foam (Pyrell replaced the DBP reference used in SAME). Across runs NASA varied heating temperature (wire resistance ratio Rt/R0 about 1.22 to 1.48; baseline, mid and high), inlet air flow (8.1 cm/s, 2 cm/s low flow, and zero flow during heating) and smoke aging time (net about 21 to 1923 s). All flight runs were in microgravity in the ISS glovebox; post-flight ground tests checked the lognormal size assumption.
investigations.relevance: SAME-R gives microgravity smoke-size data from overheated spacecraft materials for designing and judging spacecraft smoke detectors. NASA states the results are needed as the reduced-gravity baseline for future detection technology, and that size-selective or multi-moment detection could improve sensitivity and false-alarm rejection.

findings.statement: Smoke size distributions differed among the five spacecraft materials, but every material produced sub-micron particles that an ionization detector can sense.
Smoke particle sizes were log-normally distributed, mostly 100 to 600 nm, and grew substantially with longer aging and with lower air flow past the heated sample.

source.file: PSI-101_Presentations_SAME-2_Comparison of Flight and Ground Test Results.pptx

findings.statement: With no airflow during heating, smoke stayed confined to about 64 cm3 at much higher concentration and grew larger particles; NASA reports a 30 to 40 percent larger diameter of average mass across 11 zero-flow tests, with half the smoke lost through the inlet.

Smoke particles grow by nucleation, condensation and coagulation; liquid smokes (lamp wick, silicone, Kapton) coalesce while solid smokes (Teflon, Pyrell) form fractal agglomerates, and aging mainly removes the smallest particles.

Ground tests at 8 cm/s airflow gave particle sizes very close to the flight results; the ISS scattering detector performed worse for Kapton and Teflon smoke, and the Shuttle ionization detector slightly better.

findings.statement: A smoke detector that senses one moment of the size distribution is unlikely to be sensitive across all smoke sizes while resisting false alarms; detectors that normalise concentration for particle size may solve this.

investigations.title: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.objective: One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment.

needs.basis: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R).

investigations.how_tests_differ: SAME heated five materials below ignition in the ISS glovebox: Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose lamp wick and a dibutyl phthalate (DBP) reference. The plan varied air flow (5 or 10 cm/s), weight-loss rate (1 or 2 mg/min) and aging time (1 or 20 min); the flight used about 2 to 8 cm/s airflow and aging of 10 to 1800 s, with DBP points repeated. The metadata approach text matches the earlier CSD shuttle procedure (igniter 15 to 60 s, thermophoretic probes).
investigations.relevance: SAME supplies the reduced-gravity smoke-size baseline NASA says is needed to evaluate current and future spacecraft smoke detectors. Its results argue for multi-moment or size-selective detection to catch sub-micron smoke while rejecting dust, and its Destiny modelling shows obstructions and stowage change detection times.

findings.statement: A substantial portion of the smoke particles from the overheated spacecraft materials was smaller than 500 nm.
The AIAA 2008 paper included in the report concludes that low-gravity count mean diameters were about 50 percent larger, yet still below 300 nm.

Holding smoke in the aging chamber let particles coagulate: for spacecraft materials number counts fell by a factor of 1.7 to 2.7 over 800 s, count mean diameters grew about 1.5 times, and coagulation coefficients were repeatable.
Size distributions depended on the material: Kapton and Teflon smokes had narrow distributions, while silicone rubber and lamp wick smokes had broad ones.
Zero-gravity smoke transport modelling of the US Lab module showed that mixing dominates, so smoke detection lags are longer than in normal gravity.

Combining SAME with the earlier CSD results, the team concludes that detecting smoke over this size range while rejecting dust likely needs a detector that measures several moments or classifies particle size.

investigations.title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
investigations.objective: Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity. Specific objectives of this investigation were: 1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base. 2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters. 3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability. 4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions. 5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames.

needs.basis: Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.

investigations.how_tests_differ: Gas-jet flames were ignited manually from exchangeable burner tubes in the fan-driven coflow of air of the glovebox flow duct. Tests varied the fuel and its nitrogen dilution (pure methane, methane at 70% and 40% in nitrogen, ethylene at 20% in nitrogen), the burner diameter and the coflow velocity. The record lists no change of oxygen or pressure; some test days were pyrometry or fan calibrations.
investigations.relevance: NASA names insights into flame stability and behaviour that enhance fire safety as one SLICE impact, but its other stated impacts concern combustion models, soot emissions and cleaner engines on Earth. The documents given contain no result that applies SLICE to a spacecraft fire scenario.

findings.statement: NASA's hypothesis is that the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity depend strongly on burner diameter, coflow velocity and fuel composition, and are fundamentally different from flames on Earth.

NASA lists insights into flame stability and behaviour that enhance fire safety among SLICE's impacts, alongside improved numerical flame models, soot understanding for low-emission design, and cleaner engines and industrial burners.

The test log makes nitrogen dilution of the fuel the main fuel variable, from pure methane down to 40% methane and 20% ethylene, all in air coflow; with no oxygen or pressure variation recorded, the data describe ordinary-air conditions only.

Liftoff limits mark when a gas-jet flame detaches from its source; for spacecraft this could bear on whether a flame at a leaking gas line stays anchored in ventilation flow, but the documents given report no limits.

investigations.title: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.objective: The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments. Specific objectives were: (1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity. (2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points. (3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures. (4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions. (5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space.

needs.basis: Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
needs.inference: the atlas's, not NASA's: the documents do not mention smoke detection

investigations.how_tests_differ: Laminar jet diffusion flames burned in an air co-flow duct in the ISS glovebox. NASA varied fuel (ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene diluted with nitrogen to 75 and 50 percent; methane gave no smoke points), burner diameter (0.41, 0.76 and 1.6 mm), co-flow air velocity (5.4 to 65 cm/s) and fuel flow rate, which was adjusted to find each smoke point. Normal-gravity tests with the SPICE module and an unconfined 13.7 mm burner gave comparison data.
investigations.relevance: NASA states that non-buoyant smoke-point data are needed for spacecraft fire safety and frames SPICE around soot generation and oxidation in such flames. The documents do not say whether the results serve detection, prevention or suppression.

findings.statement: Faster co-flow and smaller burners lengthen non-buoyant smoke points; the final report scales smoke-point length with burner diameter to the power -0.91 and co-flow velocity to the power 0.41.
The ISS smoke points give a fuel sooting order of propane, ethylene, 50 percent propylene, 75 percent propylene and propylene.

findings.statement: Smoke-point flame length is proportional to fuel mass flow rate, with only a second-order effect of the co-flow to fuel velocity ratio.
A simplified residence-time analysis fails to collapse the smoke-point data, and no mechanism for the co-flow and burner effects is proven.

findings.statement: In non-buoyant flames soot forms near the cool core rather than near the flame sheet as in buoyant flames, and the earlier LSP experiment showed the microgravity smoke point can be dominated by radiative loss and tip extinction.

Faster co-flow raises the fuel flow a flame can carry before emitting soot, so a gas-jet fire in stronger ventilation could grow larger while releasing little smoke for detectors; SPICE did not test detection.

investigations.title: Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
investigations.hardware: ACME burner flames in the CIR
investigations.objective: 1. Plan and support flight testing on the International Space Station (ISS). 2. Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames; and a broad range of Zst, Tad, and fluent flow rate. 3. Support the flight tests with advanced CFD simulations. 4. Identify or develop a chemical kinetics mechanism that yields good agreement between the CFD predictions and the ISS measurements. 5. Disseminate the results as widely as possible.

needs.basis: Determine the conditions for which cool diffusion flames occur for propane, n-butane, and n-pentane; normal and inverse flames
needs.inference: the atlas's, not NASA's: the documents do not link CFI-G to fire safety

investigations.how_tests_differ: Spherical diffusion flames burned on a 6.35 mm porous sphere in the constant-volume CIR chamber. Tests varied fuel (ethane, propane, n-butane; ethane replaced the planned n-pentane), flame type (normal, fuel from the burner; inverse, oxidizer from the burner), fuel and oxygen fractions with nitrogen dilution, pressure (about 0.5 to 3 atm) and burner flow rate. In all, 280 hot flames were ignited over 23 test days, and cool flames were sought after radiative extinction.
investigations.relevance: The documents frame CFI-G around engine efficiency and cool-flame kinetics, not fire safety. Its fire-safety value is showing that radiatively extinguished gas flames can continue as cool flames and reignite, notably near hot platinum, in conditions mapped by fuel, oxygen, pressure and flow.

findings.statement: Spherical gas-fuelled cool diffusion flames were observed for the first time, but only for normal n-butane flames at about 2 bar and an oxygen mole fraction of about 0.39.
Cool flames arose from hot flames: of 280 hot flames, 189 went out by radiative extinction and 15 reignited as cool flames, which were identified from radiant heat flux.
A platinum (type-B) thermocouple near the flame catalysed low-temperature reactions, so hot flames that quenched reignited repeatedly through low-temperature combustion.
Cool flames were hard to initiate and to discern during operations, and scripted tests were sometimes terminated before anyone knew a cool flame was present.
Inverse n-butane flames burned steadily at the higher fuel concentration but showed large radiation oscillations and self-extinction at the lower one.

A gas flame that goes out radiatively in microgravity may not stay out: a lingering cool flame, helped by hot catalytic metal, could relight it, so suppression checks and re-ignition prevention should not rely on loss of visible flame alone.
